attribution.note: Marcus states and endorses the limitation in his own words.

semantics.note: The surrounding discussion supports a present limitation in reliable abstraction. The tool-free qualifier is preserved; the separate possibility of hybrids does not hedge this assertion.

contract.note: Continuing unreliability on multiplication beyond training coverage is a fair ordinary reading. The contract appropriately avoids treating this as permanent impossibility or absence of progress.

evidence.note: Contemporary controlled experiments report poor multiplication transfer as complexity increases despite nearly perfect familiar-case performance.
Priming demonstrates progress, but includes target-length training examples. It does not establish reliable multiplication at excluded operand lengths.

reviews.rationale: The contemporary experiments support the contracted behavioral limitation: tool-free multiplication remained unreliable beyond training coverage. Priming results do not meet the unseen-length contradiction criterion. This does not establish a universal absence of internal algorithms.

attribution.note: Marcus makes the historical comparison himself and endorses the continuing weakness.

semantics.note: The proposition faithfully captures a continuing weakness in abstract rule learning. It does not assert that every architecture fails every abstraction task.

contract.note: Reading the comparison as persistence of a behavioral weakness is ordinary and fair. Neither identical internal mechanisms nor universal failure is necessary.

evidence.note: Declining arithmetic accuracy is relevant, but training included the longer digit ranges. This does not cleanly establish failure to transfer to held-out sizes or structures.

Strong transfer to ten and fifteen digits qualifies the claim, but collapse at twenty digits and absolute-position models' failures directly demonstrate persistent limitations beyond training lengths.

reviews.rationale: The controlled addition study shows both substantial neural rule transfer and continuing failures on unfamiliar lengths. That supports persistence of a weakness under the fair contract, while ruling out an absolute inability reading. The evidence does not establish unchanged internal mechanisms across decades.
